data.title: Pfizer inks $2.6bn autoimmune deal with China’s Starna for CAR-T therapies
data.description:
In the same week that Pfizer’s CEO Albert Bourla reiterated China’s growing role in the global pharma industry, the company has ventured to the nation to sign a multi-billion-dollar licensing agreement with Starna Therapeutics focusing on CAR-T therapeutics.

As per the deal, Pfizer is paying $330m upfront to secure ex-China rights to three in vivo CAR-T programmes that are focused on treating autoimmune diseases. Starna is also in line to receive up to $2.3bn in development and commercial milestones, as well as royalties on net sales from any products arising from the partnership.

Pfizer remained tight-lipped on the programme specifics, though it confirmed the three are at the “pre-IND” phase. The drugmaker also confirmed it has acquired rights to use the Chinese biotech’s proprietary in vivo CAR-T technology in inflammation and immunology, and in oncology. Pfizer will be able to exclusively license compounds created under a separate research collaboration and an option to expand the territory to Greater China rights.

Pfizer has previous experience developing ex vivo CAR-T therapies, primarily via licensing agreements with Cellectis and Servier. But the move to bolster its pipeline with in vivo CAR-T candidates echoes a wider industry trend. In vivo is considered more attractive because it removes manufacturing complexities and scalability hurdles.

Eli Lilly has already acquired two in vivo CAR-T developers this year. In February, it spent $2.4bn to take over Orna Therapeutics and then in April outlaid $7bn in its buyout of Kelonia. Johnson & Johnson (J&J) and Moderna have also conducted deals targeting the modality this year.

Pfizer’s chief inflammation and immunology officer Michael Vincent said: “In vivo CAR-T is an emerging and promising approach for treating autoimmune diseases, and the patients who might benefit most are those for whom today’s options fall short. Pfizer has significant experience in developing and manufacturing RNA-based medicines globally, and Starna’s in vivo CAR-T programmes and technology give us a powerful way to pursue these approaches.”

Earlier this week, Pfizer’s CEO Albert Bourla alluded to China’s growing influence on drug innovation. Speaking at the Jefferies Global Healthcare Conference in London on 17 November, Bourla said that competition is set to move away from the traditional opposition of a Western big pharma company amid China’s significant growth in recent years.

While traditional licensing deals – like Pfizer and Starna’s – are still being conducted, an increased focus on national security policies in the US means other types of transactions could be curtailed.

data.title: Bridging gaps in rare disease drug access requires strategic rethink
data.description:
Over the past decade, there have been several core scientific and technological developments that have paved the way for a rare disease revolution – with new therapeutic modalities, in silico modelling and the growing access to genomic sequencing all demonstrating potential in facilitating treatment. 

However, therapeutic advancements mean nothing to patients who cannot receive them, as issues around access and reimbursement, as well as regulatory and economic hurdles continue to plague individuals with rare diseases. 

These challenges were raised from a very personal perspective by ex-UK prime minister David Cameron and Julia Vitarello, founder and CEO of Mila’s Miracle Foundation, during a fireside chat at the 2026 DIA-MHRA Global Summit, held during the London Life Sciences Week. 

During the session, Cameron and Vitarello each shared their experiences as parents of Ivan and Mila, two children with rare diseases who both sadly passed away following their battles with Ohtahara syndrome and Batten disease, respectively. While no treatment was available to Ivan for his condition during his life, Mila did eventually secure access to a therapy catered to her specific mutation – a feat that Vitarello called a “Herculean effort”. 

“My daughter received a medicine one year later, after a fight with the Boston Children’s Hospital, that became the first individualised medicine in the world,” Vitarello commented, adding that Mila set a record in the world that has “snowballed into where we are today”. 

However, Vitarello caveated that Mila’s case is exceptional, as a lion’s share of children with rare diseases are unable to access potentially life-saving drugs for their condition. 

Throughout the DIA-MHRA Global Summit, speakers were laser-focused on addressing the access gap in rare diseases – with discourse primarily turning to the need for regulatory reform, further encouragement of technological advancements, patient-centric clinical trial design and the role of data in guiding treatment and therapeutic development. 

The role of technology in boosting rare disease access 

Currently, the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution is fundamentally changing the paradigm in drug discovery and development. However, speakers noted the technology’s role does not stop there, as it can also be used across a plethora of applications in the rare disease space.  

According to Professor Fyodor Urnov, director of therapeutic R&D at the Innovative Genomics Institute (IGI) and a professor in the department of molecular & cell biology at UC Berkeley, who was involved in the creation of the treatment for Baby KJ, the field has come a long way in a short time with AI. Currently, he says it takes around a month to design a clinic-grade editor for a specific mutation across immune and metabolic diseases, as well as conditions of the blood, liver, and skin. 

“We have collaborations with Anthropic and OpenAI to limit that time,” Urnov commented, noting that AI in the future will be able to design an editor in as little as 12 hours – a potential revolution in treatment for patients with monogenic rare diseases. 

Cameron also touched upon this, adding that advancements in research and treatment driven by a combination of genomics and AI will allow the Milas and Ivans of the future to be managed by the healthcare system in a completely different way. “Not all patients will get a treatment, but they may get a better diagnosis, and we can understand more why a rare disease has happened and where it came from,” Cameron commented.  

According to the CEO of the Saudi Food and Drug Administration (SFDA), Professor Hisham Aljadhey, in silico modelling will also play a key role in scaling treatments for rare diseases. In a talk, CSO of MedGenie, Professor Michael von Forstner, noted that digital twins are also set to revolutionise the rare disease setting, as they can overcome the challenging and potentially unethical hurdle of randomising patients in clinical trials.  

“There are approaches to use digital twins in rare diseases that combine the input of data, modelling, and personalisation on the individual patient in order to build models that predict the outcomes that could happen in an individual child if they get a sample treatment,” Forstner commented. 

On top of its potential to uncover disease mechanisms to guide treatment, Kevin Lee, director and CEO of UK biotech, Bicycle Therapeutics, noted that the debut of such technologies into discovery, development, clinical trials and manufacturing could help to bring down treatment costs in the future by streamlining processes across the value chain. 

Thinking about research design and data collection 

For researchers to pursue the most productive avenues in rare disease development, experts also point to the need to improve research design and promote widespread data collection. 

On the research design side of the equation, Chris Hollowood, CEO and chief investment officer of Syncona Investment Management, noted that there should be more flexibility around p-values in rare disease.  

“If you’ve taken a gene insertion that sits on a platform that’s already been to clinic in a monogenic recessive disorder, that p-value should not be 0.05. If the regulators give us staggered p-values on a platform basis, first approved 0.05, second 0.1, third 0.15, that reduces the risk so it can actually become commercial,” Hollowood commented. 

Alongside an evolving approach to trial design, experts also pointed to the need to collate as much data as possible on rare disease populations through initiatives like newborn genomic screening outside of the context of rare disease with approved therapies. 

Focusing only on diseases with available treatment options is a mistake, Cameron believes, as screening for a broader range of rare conditions would help to collate data and build a resource that he says would greatly benefit both researchers and parents of patients. He also highlights the potential of using said data to recruit patients into clinical trials, as identifying eligible patient populations in rare disease trials can be a major bottleneck. 

Targeting regulatory reform for rare diseases

While science and technology may be advancing at a rapid pace, Vitarello and Cameron warned that the regulatory landscape is not keeping pace. They make this remark as global regulators increasingly acknowledge that their approaches applied to more common diseases are neither feasible nor sustainable for rare disease drugs.  

To tackle this challenge, the UK’s Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has debuted the Rare Disease Framework, which sets out to create a more flexible, risk-proportionate approach to rare disease development to improve access. In a panel, Urnov stressed that risk proportionality is a key consideration in rare disease regulation, and that the severity and patient burden of many rare conditions justify more flexibility in regulation. 

Aside from the Rare Disease Framework, the MHRA is also working closely with the UK’s health watchdog, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), through its aligned pathway. Through this initiative, the pair hope to bring medicines to patients up to six months sooner by converging regulatory and National Health Service (NHS) payer decision-making across Britain.

data.title: Genomics, Vertex extend drug discovery alliance in $220m deal
data.description:
Vertex Pharmaceuticals and Genomics have agreed a four-year extension to their drug discovery partnership in a deal with a potential value exceeding $220m.

The transaction builds upon a drug target discovery and validation partnership that first commenced between the two companies in 2018.

Financial terms include potential payments tied to the achievement of specified research, development, regulatory, and commercial milestones.

In addition to milestone payments, the agreement involves tiered royalties on future net sales of any therapeutic products resulting from the partnership.

The renewed collaboration focuses on applying human genetics to discover and validate new drug targets and assist with biomarker selection for precision medicines.

Researchers from Vertex Pharmaceuticals and Genomics will continue working closely together to integrate human genetic variation into research and development, aiming to better understand disease mechanisms where substantial unmet patient needs remain.

Vertex Pharmaceuticals executive vice-president and chief scientific officer Mark Bunnage said: “A deep understanding of human genetics and the underlying causal biology of diseases is foundational to how we discover and develop transformational therapies at Vertex.

“Over nearly a decade together, Genomics has proven to be an exceptional partner, combining sophisticated data science with deep genetic insights, and I’m delighted to be extending our productive partnership.”

Genomics is a transatlantic company founded in 2014 as a spin-out from the University of Oxford. Over the past decade, the business has collected, harmonised, and quality-controlled a large human genotype-phenotype database.

Genomics co-founder and CEO professor Peter Donnelly said: “Our unique platform and our proprietary algorithms allow us to bring the full power of human genetics to understand key biological processes driving disease and to use those insights to find novel targets and powerful biomarkers.” 

In July this year, Vertex signed a definitive agreement to purchase Crinetics Pharmaceuticals in a transaction valued at nearly $10bn.

data.title: FDA approves Regeneron’s Livsayis for generalised myasthenia gravis
data.description:
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved Regeneron Pharmaceuticals’ Livsayis (cemdisiran) to treat generalised myasthenia gravis (gMG) in adult patients positive for anti-acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies.

Administered subcutaneously four times annually, the therapy is a small interfering RNA designed to decrease circulating complement component factor 5 protein levels and curb terminal complement activation.

The regulatory clearance was based on findings from the ongoing randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase III NIMBLE study (NCT05070858) evaluating the treatment in individuals maintaining discretionary background immunosuppressants.

At 24 weeks, the recipients recorded a 4.5-point improvement on the Myasthenia Gravis-Activities of Daily Living scores versus 2.2 points for placebo, demonstrating a statistically significant 2.3-point difference.

The patients also displayed earlier functional gains within two weeks, with 76.6% achieving at least a 3-point improvement at week 24 compared to 44.1% on placebo.

In the clinician-administered Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis assessment, the medicine produced a 4.2-point improvement compared with 1.5 points for placebo, yielding an adjusted gain of 2.8 points.

A 5-point or greater improvement occurred in 48.4% of treated patients against 19.0% on placebo, with symptom control continuing throughout the 24-week period without diminished efficacy.

Adverse reactions affecting at least 5% of patients included injection site reactions, urinary tract infections, and viral infections.

Regeneron board co-chair, president and chief scientific officer George Yancopoulos said: “Livsayis is Regeneron’s first approved medicine in neurology, and an important new option for people living with generalised myasthenia gravis who need effective disease control without a heavy treatment burden.

“As Regeneron’s first approved siRNA therapy, this approval marks a meaningful step forward for our neuroscience pipeline as we relentlessly pursue bold, new approaches to transform care for people living with serious neurological diseases.”

Regeneron manages the therapy’s manufacturing, commercialisation, and clinical progression under a global agreement with Alnylam, while facilitating patient access and benefit verification via its myRARE programme.

Health authorities in the European Union are currently reviewing the treatment, with a decision expected during late 2027, alongside planned submissions in additional territories, including Japan.

Last month, Regeneron agreed to a nearly $270m contract extension to supply its Ebola therapy, Inmazeb, to the US Government through 2031.

data.title: European capital markets require efforts to attract biotech listings
data.description:
European capital markets are banking on reforms to position themselves as an attractive opportunity amidst a biopharma sector resurgence in 2026.

During a panel discussion at the 2026 Jefferies Global Healthcare Conference in London, taking place 16–19 November, life sciences lawyers and investors highlighted the challenging investment climate for biotechs in European markets, but a few pointed to moves made by some countries to entice international investment.

Jacqueline Mercier, partner at Goodwin, cited a statistic that of the 67 European biotechs to complete initial public offerings (IPOs) in the last six years, 66 have done so via stock exchanges outside of Europe. Regarding what this says about the European market’s credibility, fellow Goodwin partner Andrew Harrow said, “people are voting with their feet”.

Ongoing efforts to turn the tide

Amidst this environment, Harrow noted that London (and the UK) as an example of a market currently undergoing a transition. Turning away from its traditional focus on areas like mining and finances, he said London exchanges are turning their attention to the pool of high-growth companies found in biotech.

“There is a renewed focus on listing reform,” Harrow said. He pointed to reforms introduced by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) in 2024 to remove financial history requirements for companies to list their stock in the UK. “These building blocks are being put in place for London to come back as a potential venue for biotech listings,” he said.

Another issue faced more broadly in Europe compared to the US is its fractured capital markets, according to Søren Møller, managing investment director of seed investment at Novo Holdings. Møller points to the Nordic Compass as an effort to counter this weakness; this alliance of Nordic companies, investors, and others seeks more aligned capital markets across the Nordics.

Nordic biotechs like Solna, Sweden-based OneCarbon and CuraCell have previously told Pharmaceutical Technology about the difficulty companies in the region have in securing investment, according to their respective CEOs Ana Slipicevic and Jonas Båtelson. Rasmus Malmborg, special advisor at the Norwegian state initiative Innovation Norway, would like to see more specialist investors fund Nordic biotech, and in turn encourage generalist investors to do the same.

Hopefully, this sort of alignment of capital markets will spread further across Europe, said Jesper Wilkhund, CBO of Cinclus Pharma, at Jefferies. However, he added that the US is nonetheless seen as the better option for European companies to land an IPO, so it’s up to European drug developers to slowly build the credibility needed to attract US investors to come to Europe.

While the European capital market environment leaves much to be desired, opportunities for biotechs to raise funds in private markets persist. In Q2 2026, British biotechs raised £2.11bn ($2.84bn) in equity financing of which £2.05bn was from venture capital (VC) sources, as per a BioIndustry Association Report.

Against this backdrop, Bionyra Pharma’s CEO Frédéric Marrache told Pharmaceutical Technology there is still significant investment to be found in Europe. The biotech raised France’s largest Series A round for the sector in June 2026 with €143 ($165m), backed in part by Paris, France-based investors Sofinnova and Jeito. Marrache added that France is home to a range of pharma and biotech companies, investors, and sovereign wealth funds—state-owned funds—ingredients for the success of Bionyra’s Series A, in his opinion.

data.title: GSK’s $10.6bn Nuvalent bet pays off with second lung cancer drug approval
data.description:
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved GSK’s Nelkarmi (neladalkib) in lung cancer, marking the second product from the British pharma’s $10.6bn takeover of Nuvalent to reach market.

The accelerated approval is for the treatment of adults with locally advanced or metastatic anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK)-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Eligible patients are those who have previously been treated with other ALK inhibitors. Roche’s Alecensa (alectinib) is one of the most widely used ALK blockers for lung cancer.

Nelkarmi’s green light was based on results from the Phase I/II ALKOVE-1 (NCT05384626) trial. For patients previously treated with Alecensa, the confirmed overall response rate (ORR) was 49%, with 52% of responses having a duration of at least a year.

GSK’s chief scientific officer, Tony Wood, said: “Nelkarmi is our second new medicine approved in lung cancer this year. It was designed to help address key challenges of ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer through its broad coverage of ALK resistance mutations, ability to cross the blood-brain barrier and high target selectivity.

“ALK-positive patients are often younger and can remain on treatment for years, making effective and tolerable new treatment options especially important, and we are pleased to bring this innovation to patients in the US.”

Before 2026, GSK had never had a medicine specifically approved for treating lung cancer in the US. Now it has two courtesy of the Nuvalent deal that closed in mid-July. A week after the deal was signed, the FDA approved Jideytro (zidesamtinib) for patients with previously treated ROS1-positive NSCLC. This marked the first drug approved from Nuvalent’s portfolio, though analysts expect Nelkarmi to reach higher commercial heights given its larger patient population.

Analysis by GlobalData’s Pharma Intelligence Centre forecasts sales of $1.2bn in 2032 for Nelkarmi, while Jideytro is expected to make $830m in the same year. Roche’s Alecensa, which generated $1.85bn in 2025, will be a main competitor to Nelkarmi.

GlobalData is the parent company of Pharmaceutical Technology.

However, Citi analysts caveated that entry into the first-line setting remains the key value driver. Any label expansion will hinge on results from the ongoing ALKAZAR Phase III study (NCT06765109) evaluating the drug in TKI-naïve patients.

data.title: Isomorphic Labs raises $5bn to advance drug pipeline
data.description:
Isomorphic Labs has raised $5bn in a Series C financing round to support the development of its AI platform and advance its therapeutic candidates towards clinical evaluation.

Sequoia Capital and Greenoaks co-led the oversubscribed round, with additional participation from Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) and other new investors. Alphabet maintained its backing with continued investment.

The round also included existing investors CapitalG, GV, MGX, Temasek, Thrive Capital, and the UK Sovereign AI Fund.

The company will use the capital to scale its drug design engine, IsoDDE, and expand its pipeline of drug candidates.

IsoDDE brings together foundational simulation models designed to function across multiple therapeutic areas and drug modalities to identify and refine molecules with drug-like properties.

Isomorphic Labs has reported positive preclinical findings across collaborative projects as well as internal programmes in immunology and oncology, preparing the pipeline for initial clinical testing.

Isomorphic Labs founder and CEO Demis Hassabis said: “When we founded Isomorphic, our conviction was that biology could be understood and modelled at the most fundamental molecular level and radically accelerated through AI. Our drug design engine is generating molecules with unprecedented precision and speed.

“This round enables us to accelerate our progress: building foundational biology models, deepening our systemic disease understanding, and driving our first therapeutic programmes towards clinical trials to deliver tangible impact for patients.”

Proceeds from the financing will also fund translational and clinical development infrastructure as drug candidates move towards trials.

In addition, the company is establishing a partner network to improve understanding of mechanistic disease biology, whilst building global infrastructure to support its bioengineering and computational biology operations.

Chris Molloy, CEO of the BioIndustry Association (BIA), said in an email to Pharmaceutical Technology: “Isomorphic Labs’ £3.8bn ($5bn) investment ​is not only a new peak for UK-founded companies; it is the largest ever venture capital raise for life sciences globally. This is a powerful vote of confidence in UK life sciences and a strong endorsement for our TechBio sector. Bringing breakthrough AI and drug discovery together offers extraordinary potential to tackle diseases that still lack effective treatments.

“When companies with exceptional science receive exceptional backing, it enables them to grow, scale and serve the world from here. Britain should be a place where it is common for scientific breakthroughs to become global businesses and, ultimately, life-changing medicines.”

In March 2025, the company raised $600m in its first external funding round as it pushes forward with AI-driven drug discovery.

data.title: Revolution Medicines’ Rasonque gains EC authorisation for pancreatic cancer
data.description:
The European Commission (EC) has granted marketing authorisation for Revolution Medicines’ Rasonque (daraxonrasib) to treat adult patients with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma who have undergone at least one systemic therapy earlier.

The decision permits use of the once-daily oral tablet in individuals with or without an identified RAS tumour mutation.

Rasonque is a RAS(ON) multi-selective, noncovalent, tri-complex inhibitor.

The marketing authorisation applies to all European Union (EU) member states and the European Economic Area (EEA) nations Liechtenstein, Iceland, and Norway.

It does not cover Switzerland or the UK, both of which maintain independent regulatory frameworks.

Patient availability will vary by jurisdiction, depending on the completion of national pricing, health-technology assessment, and procedures related to reimbursement.

Revolution Medicines CEO and chairman Mark Goldsmith said: “Today’s European Commission approval of Rasonque represents a pivotal moment for people in the European Union living with metastatic pancreatic cancer, as well as their families.

“With Rasonque now approved, we are actively working with healthcare systems and stakeholders across the region to support timely access for eligible patients.

“We also continue to engage with regulatory authorities around the world with the goal of expanding and accelerating the reach of rasonque to patients who may benefit from it.”

The approval follows a positive opinion issued by the Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) of the European Medicines Agency (EMA). The assessment took place under an expedited phased review within the EMA’s Cancer Medicines Pathfinder project, reflecting the therapy’s potential to address high unmet medical need.

The EC authorisation was underpinned by data from the global Phase III RASolute 302 registrational trial (NCT06625320), published in The New England Journal of Medicine and presented at the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology Annual Meeting.

RASolute 302 compared a daily 300mg dose of rasonque monotherapy against an investigator’s choice of four cytotoxic chemotherapy regimens in previously treated patients.

The study met all primary and key secondary endpoints in both the overall intent-to-treat (ITT) group and patients harbouring RAS G12 mutations.

Rasonque holds approval from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for adults with metastatic disease who have received prior systemic therapy or cannot receive multiagent regimens.

Earlier this week at the Jefferies Global Healthcare Conference in London, Goldsmith discussed the commercial rollout strategy for American patients.

Revolution Medicines is also evaluating it in global Phase III registrational trials for metastatic RAS-mutant non-small cell lung cancer and pancreatic cancer.

In August this year, BeOne Medicines signed a multi-part collaboration with Revolution Medicines to develop and commercialise targeted oncology therapies.

data.title: Eli Lilly inks cancer pact worth up to $5.9bn with Stipple Bio
data.description:
Eli Lilly has signed an oncology research collaboration and license agreement with Stipple Bio worth up to $5.9bn as it looks to bolster its precision cancer treatment pipeline.

Stipple Bio has developed a platform it calls Pointillist that identifies novel tumour-specific cell surface epitope binders. Epitopes are the antigen components that the immune system recognises and binds to with B cells, T cells, and proteins. Stipple’s aim is to develop powerful therapies that selectively target tumour cells, reducing on-target, off-tumour toxicity while increasing efficacy.

Neither Lilly nor Stipple disclosed how the $5.9bn was split, though the transaction involves the former making an upfront payment and equity investment into the biotech.

Stipple is also in line for research, product development and commercialisation milestones, as well as tiered royalties on product sales should Lilly successfully commercialise therapies from the collaboration. Lilly will attain worldwide rights to develop and commercialise any products arising from the pair-up.

Lilly said it would combine the biotech’s work with its proprietary oncology technologies to advance high therapeutic index compounds across multiple modalities.

Stipple stated it plans to initiate a Phase I clinical trial for an antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) in early 2027 for solid tumours, including pancreatic cancer.

Stipple’s CEO Jeff Landau said: “Stipple Bio was founded with the belief that epitope-level precision could distinguish tumour cells from healthy tissue, unlocking a new generation of effective and safer cancer therapies directed at targets whose expression on healthy cells has historically limited their clinical utility.”

The research agreement marks the second deal for Lilly this week, after it spent $1.5bn to acquire rare blood cancer biotech Calytrix Bio on 16 November.

It means Lilly has maintained a near-monthly M&A presence this year. The most expensive of these was the $7.8bn takeover of sleep drugmaker Centessa Pharmaceuticals in March.

data.title: Pfizer CEO: ‘China will be my major competition by 2030’
data.description:
Pfizer’s CEO Albert Bourla forecasts that China will be his main competitor within five years, as the Asian nation implements a policy drive to cement its powerhouse role in the global drug innovation landscape.

Speaking at the Jefferies Global Healthcare Conference in London on 17 November, Bourla said that competition is set to move away from the traditional opposition of a Western big pharma company amid China’s significant growth in recent years.

He said: “China [is] growing its biotech business and has an ambition to become a global player. I think they will be successful.”

China has embarked on a strategy to grow beyond its role as a popular licensing destination in recent years. In September, the Chinese government unveiled its 15th five-year plan for its biomedical industry, with aims to be more proactive on the global stage. By 2030, China wants to make and develop 25% of global first-in-class drugs. The government said it wanted to become an exporter of innovative drugs rather than a supplier of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs).

“By 2030, they will represent my major competition. It’s not going to be AstraZeneca or Eli Lilly. It’s going to be Chinese companies,” Bourla added.

Over the past decade, China has become a go-to port of call for Western big pharma searching for pipeline additions. Licensing deals between US and Chinese biopharma companies have significantly increased over recent years, according to analysis by GlobalData, parent company of Pharmaceutical Technology. While analysis hasn’t been conducted in 2026, estimates look like another deal inflexion is on the cards. 

High-profile transactions this year include AstraZeneca’s $18.5bn obesity deal with CSPC, which was forged in January 2026, and Bristol Myers Squibb’s (BMS’s) $15.2bn deal with Jiangsu Hengrui Pharma in May 2026.

President Xi Jinping has outlined a series of initiatives to achieve this and its wider target of becoming a global pharma leader. Research and development (R&D) efforts will significantly ramp up, artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum computing will continue to be harnessed in drug discovery, and pharma ecosystems will be built beyond just pipelines.

“They are coming in at half the cost, and three or four times the speed. If we want to compete with them by 2030, we need to be half the cost, and increase speed by three or four times,” Bourla warned. “That sounds very difficult to achieve, unless AI delivers on the problems. And AI, for me, is the biggest lever to be able to build the Pfizer for the future,” he added.

Geopolitical flux raises questions

Bourla’s comments come amid a shift in political tides that play a key role in relationships between Western pharma companies and Chinese biotechs. Last month, the US Department of the Treasury proposed adding biotech to the Comprehensive Outbound Investment Security (COINS) Act. The framework expands the government’s ability to restrict or monitor US investment in sensitive technologies developed by companies listed as “ones of concern”. The Act has widely been described as primarily targeting American investment in China.

Biotech’s potential inclusion on COINS adds to a US-China pharma landscape already fraught with complications. The BIOSECURE Act came into law this year, limiting Chinese biotechs and manufacturers from accessing US funding and collaborating with domestic pharma companies using federal funds.

Then in November, a switch in US Congress arrived when the Democrats won both the Senate and the House in midterms. While analysts have said near-term pharma dynamics will largely be unaffected, this increases the focus on Trump administration policies such as China-directed investment and Most Favored Nation (MFN) deals.
